conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new mothers. I’d like to spend the next few minutes asking you the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screening that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived so we can make sure you get the right support. Everything you share is confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers. If at any point you need to pause, just let me know.

I’ll ask each question in everyday language, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. When you’re ready, we’ll begin.

Looking back over the past seven days, how often have you found moments of enjoyment or laughter—whether with your baby, family, friends, or just in little things around the house?

Honestly… it feels pretty rare. I’ll catch myself half-smiling if the baby squeezes my finger or if my toddler does something silly, but the laughter fades fast—like I’m too tired or worried to hold on to it. Most of the day I’m just going through the motions, so “enjoyment” seems like a stretch.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I mean, every now and then something small will make me crack a smile, but it’s like the laughter gets stuck. I’ll think “that should be funny,” but I can’t feel it in my chest the way I used to. Most of the time I’m too worn-out or on-edge to find the humor in anything.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much at all. When I think about tomorrow—or next week—it just feels like a long, gray tunnel of feedings, diapers, and trying to keep everyone safe. I used to get excited about little outings or even just a quiet cup of coffee, but now it’s hard to picture anything feeling truly enjoyable. I still do the things, but the “looking forward” part seems missing.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m not soothing him right or because I ate something that bothers him. When my toddler throws a tantrum I’m convinced I’m failing her too. I know, rationally, kids cry and babies fuss, but in my head it keeps circling back to “I’m just not good enough at this mom thing.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. My mind keeps jumping to awful “what-ifs”—like the baby might suddenly stop breathing, or I’ll drop him, or I’ll miss some sign that he’s sick. There’s no real reason; he’s healthy and check-ups go fine. But the tight-chest feeling shows up anyway, especially at night when the house gets quiet.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

It’s happened a few times this week. Out of nowhere my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t get a full breath—like something terrible is about to happen, even though nothing’s wrong. I’ll be rocking the baby or folding laundry and suddenly I’m sweating and have to sit down. It passes after a bit, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes—most days feel like I’m barely treading water. I’ll finally get the baby down and the toddler needs a snack, or I start a chore and the baby cries again. It piles up so fast that by dinner I’m snapping at my partner over tiny things, then crying because I hate sounding like this. I keep telling myself “just get through tonight,” but tomorrow looks the same.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening almost every night this week. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning—replaying everything I might have done wrong, worrying about the baby, feeling guilty that I’m not happier. I’ll drift off for an hour and then jolt awake, heart pounding, sure I heard him cry. After that I just stare at the ceiling until the sun starts to come up.
I have felt sad or miserable

A lot of the time. It’s like there’s this heavy blanket over me—nothing feels bright or exciting, even when things are technically fine. I’ll be feeding the baby and tears just start slipping out, or I’ll look at pictures of how happy I was before he was born and feel like I’ve lost that version of myself. The sadness comes in waves, and some days it’s hard to see past it.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah, that’s been happening. Not every single day, but a few times this week—like yesterday when the baby wouldn’t nap and I couldn’t even make lunch. I just sat on the couch with him on my chest and cried because everything felt impossible. Sometimes it’s quiet tears while I’m doing dishes, sometimes it’s full-on sobbing when I’m alone in the shower. It feels like the only way the pressure leaks out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel overwhelmed and sad, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my kids deserve.

You've shared that the past week has felt like trudging through a heavy fog: smiles fade quickly, the future looks gray, and even small tasks feel impossible. You're caring for your baby and toddler while carrying constant worry, nightly insomnia, and a steady sense of guilt. Crying offers brief release, yet the sadness returns in waves, leaving you wondering where the joyful, pre-baby version of yourself has gone.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, fleeting smiles and inability to feel genuine laughter, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete loss of anticipatory pleasure and inability to picture future events as enjoyable, matching "Hardly at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, pervasive self-blame across parenting situations, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily, intrusive, catastrophic worries without real triggers, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic with physical symptoms several times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to manage cascading demands, emotional dysregulation (snapping, crying), and sees no change ahead—closely aligns with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly sleeplessness driven by unhappiness, guilt, and anxiety, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness ('a lot of the time'), frequent crying, anhedonia, and persistent low mood—matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>"Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 24 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major depression. Endorsement of <sym>anhedonia</sym> (Q1,Q2), pervasive <sym>low mood</sym> and frequent crying (Q8,Q9), excessive self-blame (Q3), nightly insomnia driven by rumination (Q7), multiple panic attacks (Q5), and feeling unable to cope (Q6) aligns with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Absence of self-harm thoughts (Q10 score 0) is reassuring but does not diminish clinical urgency. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule urgent visit with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within the next few days
2. Ask about same-day referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> and evidence-based therapy options
3. Discuss medication compatibility with breastfeeding if applicable
4. Arrange practical support-partner, family, or postpartum doula for daytime rest and overnight help
5. Practice brief self-soothing routines (deep breathing, 5-minute shower, gentle music) when panic symptoms start
6. Limit information overload; choose one trusted parenting resource rather than late-night searching
7. Plan daily 15-minute outdoor walk with baby for natural light and gentle movement
8. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Screening note – Postpartum period, self-report

Symptoms endorsed:
- Markedly reduced ability to experience pleasure or humor (Q1, Q2)
- Daily low mood, frequent crying spells, feelings of heaviness/sadness (Q8, Q9)
- Excessive, persistent guilt and self-blame regarding parenting adequacy (Q3)
- Daily free-floating anxiety with catastrophic worries about infant safety (Q4)
- Multiple episodic panic symptoms (heart racing, breathlessness, diaphoresis) without clear precipitant (Q5)
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia driven by rumination and hypervigilance (Q7)
- Sense of being unable to cope, “treading water,” irritability (Q6)

Patterns:
- Symptoms present “most days” and “this week,” causing functional difficulty with caregiving tasks and partner interactions
- No anhedonia remission reported; insomnia worsens mood in circular fashion
- No current self-harm or suicidal ideation (Q10); therefore no acute safety alert at this time

Areas of screening significance:
- Meets threshold concerns for possible major depressive episode with peripartum onset; co-occurring anxiety/panic features noted
- Moderate–high distress; impairment in daily functioning evident
- Reassure safety plan intact; continue monitoring for any emergent self-harm thoughts

Next step:
- Recommend formal clinical interview with standardized perinatal mood/anxiety measures to clarify severity and rule out other etiologies
